slides.title: Chromosome vs plasmid
slides.oldHtml:
Circular chromosome vs plasmid

Circular chromosome (main DNA)
  • One huge loop of DNA floating free in the cytoplasm (no nucleus)
  • Carries all the essential genes the bacterium needs to survive and reproduce
  • Copied once whenever the bacterium splits in two
Plasmids (bonus DNA rings)
  • Tiny extra rings of DNA — a cell can have none, one, or many
  • Carry useful bonus genes — e.g. antibiotic resistance
  • Can be copied & passed between bacteria (and used by scientists in genetic modification)
slides.newHtml:
Chromosome vs plasmid

Circular chromosome (main DNA)
  • One huge loop of DNA free in the cytoplasm (no nucleus)
  • Carries all the essential genes needed to survive & divide
  • Copied once each time the bacterium splits in two
Plasmids (bonus DNA rings)
  • Small extra rings of DNA (none, one, or many per cell)
  • Carry bonus genes — e.g. antibiotic resistance
  • Can be copied & shared between bacteria (also used in genetic modification)

slides.title: Solids
slides.oldHtml:
Solids

Fixed positions in a regular lattice
Vibrate, more when heated
Fixed shape and volume
High density
Strong forces of attraction
slides.newHtml:
Solids

  • Fixed positions in a regular lattice
  • Vibrate about fixed positions (more when heated)
  • Fixed shape and fixed volume
  • High density — cannot be compressed
Forces of attraction: Strong

slides.title: Liquids
slides.oldHtml:
Liquids

Close together (touching), random
Move past each other
Fixed volume, takes the container's shape
Can't be compressed easily
Weak forces of attraction
slides.newHtml:
Liquids

  • Close together (touching), random arrangement
  • Move past each other (faster when heated)
  • Fixed volume, takes the shape of the container
  • Cannot be compressed easily
Forces of attraction: Weak

Gases

  • Random and far apart
  • Move freely in all directions (faster when heated)
  • No fixed shape or volume — fill any container
  • Low density — easily compressed

slides.title: Melting and freezing
slides.oldHtml:
Melting and freezing

Heating: particles vibrate more
At the melting point they break free and move around: melting
Cooling: at the freezing point they are held in place again
melting point = freezing point
slides.newHtml:
Melting and freezing

  • Heating a solid: particles vibrate more
  • At the melting point they overcome fixed positions and move around: melting
  • Cooling a liquid: at the freezing point forces hold them in place again
melting point = freezing point

slides.title: Boiling and condensing
slides.oldHtml:
Boiling and condensing

Heating a liquid: particles move faster
At the boiling point they overcome all the forces of attraction
→ spread far apart: boiling
Condensing is the opposite, caused by cooling
slides.newHtml:
Boiling and condensing

  • Heating a liquid: particles move faster
  • At the boiling point they overcome all forces of attraction
  • Particles spread far apart → boiling
Condensing: gas → liquid when cooled

slides.title: Evaporation
slides.oldHtml:
Evaporation

Liquid → gas without boiling
Particles at the surface gain enough energy to escape
Faster at higher temperature or in direct sunlight
slides.newHtml:
Evaporation

Liquid → gas without boiling
  • Fastest particles escape from the surface
  • Happens at any temperature below the boiling point
  • Boiling forms bubbles throughout the liquid at the boiling point

Sublimation: solid → gas
e.g. dry ice (solid CO2)
Deposition: gas → solid
e.g. frost forming in a freezer
slides.newHtml:
Sublimation and deposition

Sublimation: solid → gas
  • e.g. dry ice (solid CO2)
Deposition: gas → solid
  • e.g. frost forming in a freezer

slides.title: Temperature and state
slides.oldHtml:
Temperature and state

Water: melts at 0 °C, boils at 100 °C
What state is water at 24 °C?
→ liquid (it's between 0 and 100)
At exactly 0 °C or 100 °C it could be in either state
slides.newHtml:
Temperature and state

Water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.
What state is it at 24 °C?
  • Liquid — 24 °C is between 0 °C and 100 °C
  • Below 0 °C → solid; above 100 °C → gas
  • At exactly 0 °C or 100 °C, it can be in either state

slides.title: Which has stronger forces?
slides.oldHtml:
Which has stronger forces?

Air or olive oil?
Air is a gas at room temperature: its boiling point is below it (about −195 °C)
Olive oil is a liquid: its boiling point is above room temperature
Stronger forces → more energy to separate the particles → higher boiling point
slides.newHtml:
Which has stronger forces?

At room temperature (25 °C), air is a gas and olive oil is a liquid.

Weak forces (e.g. air)

Stronger forces (e.g. olive oil)
More energy needed to separate → higher boiling point
Stronger forces of attraction → more energy needed → higher boiling point

slides.title: Orbital speed
slides.newHtml:

v=2πrT
  • r = orbital radius (distance from centre)
  • T = time period (time for one full orbit)
  • Closer bodies feel stronger gravity → move faster

slides.title: Orbital speed: watch the units
slides.newHtml:
Orbital speed: watch the units

orbital speed=2 × π × orbital radiustime period
Distance in m and time in s → speed in m/s
Distance in km and time in days → speed in km/day

slides.title: Worked example: Mercury
slides.newHtml:
Worked example: Mercury

QUESTION: Mercury takes 87.97 days to orbit the Sun. Orbital radius = 57.91 million km. Find its orbital speed.
Step 1 — One orbit distance (2πr)
2 × π × 57.91 million km = 363.9 million km
Step 2 — Divide by time period (T)
363.9 million ÷ 87.97 = 4.14 million km/day
Step 3 — Convert to m/s (1 day = 86 400 s)
4 140 000 000 m ÷ 86 400 s = 47 900 m/s

slides.title: Geostationary satellites
slides.newHtml:
Geostationary satellites

Challenge
A geostationary satellite orbits once every 24 hours at height 35 000 km above Earth’s surface (Earth’s radius = 6400 km). Find its speed in m/s.
Watch the exam trap: r is from Earth’s centre!
  • r = 6400 + 35 000 = 41 400 km = 41 400 000 m
  • T = 24 × 3600 = 86 400 s
v = 2π × 41 400 000 ÷ 86 400 = 3010 m/s

slides.title: How stars are born
slides.newHtml:
How stars are born

1. Nebula
Giant cloud of hydrogen gas and dust pulled together by gravity over millions of years
2. Protostar
Collapsing core becomes hot and dense (gravitational potential → thermal energy)
3. Main sequence star
Hot enough in the core → hydrogen fusion ignites: a star is born!

Like hot metal

Heating metal
Glows red → orange → yellow → white-hot
Same rule for stars
  • Coolest stars glow red
  • Hotter stars glow yellow / white
  • The hottest stars glow blue

slides.title: Main sequence stars
slides.newHtml:
Main sequence stars

For most of a star’s life, it is stable:
Inward force
Gravity pulls all the gas inwards
Outward force
Heat & radiation pressure from hydrogen fusion push outwards
Inward gravity = Outward pressure → STABLE

slides.title: Red giants
slides.newHtml:
Red giants

When core hydrogen runs out, the star leaves the main sequence:
  • The outer layers expand enormously
  • Its surface becomes much cooler
  • Cooler surface → glows red
Later it sheds its outer layers, leaving a tiny, hot white dwarf

Supernova

A red supergiant collapses violently and explodes
  • Can outshine an entire galaxy for weeks
  • About one every 50 years in a galaxy like the Milky Way
  • Leaves behind a neutron star or a black hole
Crab Nebula — remnant of a 1054 AD supernova (Hubble)

slides.title: Black holes
slides.newHtml:
Black holes

Formed by the collapse of the most massive stars
  • All the star’s remaining mass is crushed into a tiny point
  • Gravitational field strength is unimaginably strong
Past the event horizon, not even light can escape!
